title: Imperfect subjunctive: parlés, fos, fes
explanation:
The imperfect subjunctive (imperfet de subjuntiu) is needed in subordinate clauses when the main verb is in a past tense or the conditional, and in hypothetical “if” clauses. English has almost lost its subjunctive (the last trace is if I were), so where English uses an infinitive (I wanted you to come) or a plain past (if I had time), Catalan needs a full verb form: Volia que vinguessis. Si tingués temps…

  • -ar: parlés, parlessis, parlés, parléssim, parléssiu, parlessin
  • -er/-re: perdés, perdessis, perdés, perdéssim, perdéssiu, perdessin
  • -ir: dormís, dormissis, dormís, dormíssim, dormíssiu, dormissin

Watch the accents: only the jo, ell/ella, nosaltres and vosaltres forms carry one (parlés, parléssim); parlessis and parlessin have none.

Irregular verbs generally use the stem of the simple past (passat simple):

  • ser → fos, fossis, fos, fóssim, fóssiu, fossin
  • fer → fes, fessis, fes, féssim, féssiu, fessin
  • tenir → tingués, venir → vingués, poder → pogués, voler → volgués, haver → hagués, dir → digués, estar → estigués, anar → anés, saber → sabés, viure → visqués, veure → veiés

Fos and fes are one syllable, so they take no accent. In Valencian usage, forms in -ara / -era are common (parlara, perdera, fóra); in Catalonia the -és / -ís forms are the usual ones. Both are standard.

examples.en: I wanted you to come.
If I had time, I’d do it.
I wish it were true.

examples.ca: Li vaig dir que no fes soroll.
examples.en: I told him not to make any noise.

exercises.instruction: Put the verb into the imperfect subjunctive.

title: Conditional sentences: si plou… / si plogués…
explanation:
A real condition (it may well happen): si + present, and in the main clause the present, the future or an imperative, just as in English:

  • Si plou, no sortirem. (If it rains, we won’t go out.)
  • Si tens gana, menja. (If you’re hungry, eat.)

As in English (if you come, not “if you will come”), there is no future after si: Si vens…, not “si vindràs”.

An unlikely or imaginary condition about the present: si + imperfect subjunctive → conditional:

  • Si tingués diners, viatjaria més. (If I had money, I’d travel more.)
  • Si fos tu, no ho faria. (If I were you, I wouldn’t do it.)

Two traps for English speakers. First, never put the conditional after si: “si tindria” is as wrong as “if I would have money”. Second, don’t copy the English past tense: si tenia diners (imperfect indicative) talks about a real past situation (“whenever I had money back then”), not an imaginary one. For “if I had”, say si tingués.

examples.en: If you get here early, call me.

examples.ca: Si fa bo, anirem a la platja.
examples.en: If the weather’s nice, we’ll go to the beach.

examples.ca: Si parlés català, treballaria a Barcelona.
examples.en: If I spoke Catalan, I’d work in Barcelona.

examples.ca: Què faries si guanyessis la loteria?
examples.en: What would you do if you won the lottery?

exercises.instruction: Real condition: fill in the verbs.
Imaginary condition: si + imperfect subjunctive → conditional.

items.q: Si (saber, ell) ___ la resposta, te la (dir) ___.
Si (viure, nosaltres) ___ a la costa, (anar) ___ a la platja cada dia.

title: The unreal past: si ho hagués sabut…
summary: Conditions that can no longer come true.
explanation:
For a past that can’t be changed (English if I had known, I would have…), Catalan uses si + pluperfect subjunctive (hagués + past participle) → conditional perfect (hauria + past participle):

  • Si ho hagués sabut, t’ho hauria dit. (If I’d known, I’d have told you.)
  • Si haguessis vingut, t’hauries divertit. (If you’d come, you’d have had a good time.)

Forms: hagués, haguessis, hagués, haguéssim, haguéssiu, haguessin + past participle; hauria, hauries, hauria, hauríem, hauríeu, haurien + past participle.

Careful with the English contraction I’d: it can stand for I had (→ hagués) or I would (→ hauria). Unpack it before translating, and never put hauria after si.

A mixed condition has a past cause and a present result, as in English If I had studied medicine, I’d be a doctor now: Si hagués estudiat medicina, ara seria metge.

In everyday speech the pluperfect subjunctive is often used in both halves instead of the conditional perfect: Si ho hagués sabut, t’ho hagués dit.

examples.ca: Si haguéssim sortit abans, no hauríem perdut el tren.
examples.en: If we’d left earlier, we wouldn’t have missed the train.
If you’d called me, I’d have helped you.

examples.ca: Si no hagués plogut, ara el camp estaria sec.
examples.en: If it hadn’t rained, the field would be dry now.

exercises.instruction: Put the verbs into the unreal past.

items.q: Si (saber, jo) ___ que venies, (fer) ___ un pastís.
Si (arribar, ells) ___ a temps, (veure) ___ el concert.

title: Sequence of tenses with the subjunctive
summary: Vull que vinguis → volia que vinguessis.
explanation:
English often avoids a subordinate clause altogether: I want you to come, he asked me to help him. Catalan can’t do that when the two subjects are different: it needs que + subjunctive, and the tense of that subjunctive depends on the tense of the main verb:

  • main verb in the present / future → present subjunctive: Vull que vinguis. Li diré que truqui.
  • main verb in a past tense / the conditional → imperfect subjunctive: Volia que vinguessis. M’agradaria que truqués.

Compare:

  • Em demana que l’ajudi. → Em va demanar que l’ajudés. (He asks me to help him. → He asked me to help him.)
  • Espero que estiguis bé. → Esperava que estiguessis bé. (I hope you’re well. → I hoped you were well.)

Notice that the English infinitive (to help) doesn’t change at all, so English gives you no clue: look at the Catalan main verb and match the tense.

If the action of the subordinate clause is already complete, use the perfect subjunctive (hagi fet) or the pluperfect subjunctive (hagués fet): M’alegro que hagis vingut. M’alegrava que haguessis vingut. (I’m glad you’ve come. I was glad you had come.)

examples.ca: El metge em va dir que descansés.
examples.en: The doctor told me to rest.

examples.ca: Seria millor que no hi anéssim.
examples.en: It would be better if we didn’t go.

examples.ca: No crec que ho hagi entès.
examples.en: I don’t think he’s understood.

examples.ca: Dubtava que ho haguessin fet sols.
examples.en: I doubted they had done it on their own.

exercises.instruction: Put the sentence into the past.

title: Future perfect and conditional perfect
summary: Hauré acabat, hauria vingut, and guesses about the past.
explanation:
The future perfect = hauré, hauràs, haurà, haurem, haureu, hauran + past participle. Like English will have done, it describes an action completed before a point in the future:

  • A les vuit ja hauré acabat. (I’ll have finished by eight.)

It also expresses a guess about the past, where English says must have or probably: No contesta; haurà sortit. (He isn’t answering; he must have gone out.) Also very common: deu haver sortit.

The conditional perfect = hauria, hauries, hauria, hauríem, hauríeu, haurien + past participle, English would have done: something that could have happened but didn’t:

  • Hauria vingut, però estava malalt. (I would have come, but I was ill.)
  • Hauríeu d’haver-ho dit abans. (You should have said so earlier.)

English should have / ought to have done is hauria d’haver + past participle (literally “would have to have done”). The pronoun goes either after haver or in front of the whole group: Hauríeu d’haver-ho dit = Ho hauríeu d’haver dit.

examples.en: By the time you get here, we’ll have had dinner.
Where can he have put the keys?
I would have liked to meet her.
I would never have said that.

items.q: El mes que ve ja (acabar, jo) ___ la carrera.
Amb més temps, ho (fer, nosaltres) ___ millor.
No és a casa; (anar) ___ a la feina.
(haver de, tu + trucar-me) ___! (“You should have called me!”)
items.a: Hauries d’haver-me trucat! / M’hauries d’haver trucat!

title: Prepositions that disappear before que
summary: Penso en tu / penso que… / penso anar-hi.
explanation:
Many verbs and expressions take a fixed preposition, often not the one English uses: pensar en (think about), adonar-se de (realise), acostumar-se a (get used to), estar d’acord amb (agree with), insistir en (insist on).

Before the conjunction que the unstressed prepositions a, en, amb, de drop:

  • M’adono de l’error. → M’adono que m’he equivocat. (I realise my mistake. → I realise I’ve made a mistake.)
  • Estic d’acord amb la idea. → Estic d’acord que cal canviar. (I agree with the idea. → I agree that we need to change.)
  • Insisteix en el preu. → Insisteix que paguem. (He insists on the price. → He insists that we pay.)

English does much the same (aware of the problem → aware that there’s a problem), so the rule feels natural. The difference: English can also leave out that (I’m sure she’ll come), but Catalan never drops que: Estic segur que vindrà.

Before an infinitive, en and amb change to a or drop, while a and de stay. Where English has a preposition + -ing (insist on paying), Catalan has a preposition + infinitive:

  • Insisteix a pagar. (He insists on paying.) Es va comprometre a venir. (She committed to coming.)
  • M’alegro de veure’t. (I’m glad to see you.) M’he acostumat a llevar-me d’hora. (I’ve got used to getting up early.)

Note also pensar en “think about”, but pensar + infinitive, with no preposition, “plan to”: Penso anar-hi demà.

This is one of the most noticeable features of standard Catalan: it’s often ignored in speech, but it’s checked in writing.

examples.en: I’m glad you came.
I’m sure she’ll come.
I’m planning to go there tomorrow.
I trust everything will be fine.

exercises.instruction: Fill in the preposition, or leave the gap empty.

items.q: Estic d’acord ___ que ho fem així.

title: Verbal periphrases: acabar de, tornar a, deixar de…
summary: Verb + preposition + infinitive with a new meaning.
explanation:
• acabar de + inf. (have just): Acabo d’arribar. (I’ve just arrived.)
  • tornar a + inf. (again): Torna a ploure. (It’s raining again.)
  • deixar de + inf. (stop doing): He deixat de fumar. (I’ve stopped smoking.)
  • començar a / posar-se a + inf. (start; posar-se a: suddenly): Es va posar a plorar. (She burst into tears.)
  • estar a punt de + inf. (be about to): El tren està a punt de sortir. (The train is about to leave.)
  • soler + inf. (usually): Solem sopar a les nou. (We usually have dinner at nine.) In the past it means “used to”: Solia anar-hi a peu. (I used to walk there.)
  • anar + gerund (gradually): La situació va millorant. (Things are gradually getting better.)
  • continuar / seguir + gerund (keep doing, still): Continua treballant aquí. (He still works here.)

Tense trap: acabar de is in the present where English uses the present perfect (Acabo d’arribar, “I’ve just arrived”), and in the imperfect for English “had just” (Acabava d’arribar, “I had just arrived”). Don’t translate this “just” as només, which means “only”.

Don’t confuse acabar de (“have just”) with acabar + noun (“finish”): Acabo la feina (I’m finishing work).

examples.en: We’ve just had lunch.
Don’t do that again!
I was just about to call you.
He’s usually late.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Catalan using a periphrasis.

items.a: Ha tornat a oblidar les claus.

items.q: We’ve stopped going to the gym.
The concert is about to start.
items.a: El concert està a punt de començar.

items.q: She usually has breakfast at home.

title: Gerund clauses and en + infinitive
explanation:
A gerund at the start of a sentence expresses a simultaneous action, manner or cause, much like an English -ing clause:

  • Caminant per la platja, vaig trobar una ampolla. (Walking along the beach, I found a bottle.)
  • Sent tan tard, millor que no hi anem. (It being so late, we’d better not go.)

But the Catalan gerund can’t describe an action that comes after the main one, although English allows it (The storm hit the coast, causing a lot of damage). “Va sortir, tancant la porta” is wrong; say Va sortir i va tancar la porta.

Also, an English -ing form used as a noun is an infinitive in Catalan: Reading is fun is Llegir és divertit, not “Llegint és divertit”.

En + infinitive means “when, as soon as”. It’s the exact equivalent of formal English on + -ing: En arribar a casa, em vaig dutxar. (On arriving home, I had a shower.)

A participle clause expresses an action completed before the main one: Acabat el sopar, vam sortir. (Dinner over, we went out.) Un cop fets els deures, pots jugar. (Once your homework is done, you can play.) The participle agrees with its noun: acabat el sopar, acabada la reunió, fets els deures.

examples.ca: En sortir de la feina, vaig anar al mercat.
examples.en: On leaving work, I went to the market.
You learn a lot by reading.

examples.ca: Un cop acabada la reunió, ens en vam anar.
examples.en: Once the meeting was over, we left.

examples.ca: Tenint en compte la situació, ho deixarem per demà.
examples.en: Given the situation, we’ll leave it until tomorrow.

items.q: Quan va arribar, va trucar a la seva mare.
items.a: En arribar, va trucar a la seva mare.

items.q: Quan vam veure el preu, vam marxar.
items.a: En veure el preu, vam marxar.

exercises.instruction: Correct or not? If not, correct it.

items.q: Va entrar a casa, encenent el llum.
items.a: Not correct: Va entrar a casa i va encendre el llum.

title: Diminutive and augmentative suffixes
explanation:
English has only a handful of diminutive endings (doggie, booklet, kitchenette) and usually just says little or tiny. Catalan uses suffixes all the time, and they often express affection rather than actual size.

Diminutive suffixes:

  • -et / -eta, the most common: noi → noiet, casa → caseta, gat → gatet, poc → poquet
  • -ó / -ona, mostly with adjectives: petit → petitó, petitona

Augmentative suffixes, often admiring or scornful:

  • -às / -assa: cotxe → cotxàs (a massive car), casa → casassa (a huge house)
  • -ot / -ota: gran → grandot (big and hulking), noi → noiot (a big lad)

The suffix agrees in gender, the final vowel of the base drops (casa → caseta), and the spelling of the stem changes to keep the pronunciation: poc → poquet, boca → boqueta, because c before e would sound like s. The accent on -às and -ó disappears when an ending is added: cotxassos, petitona.

Many former diminutives have become separate words with their own meaning: llibret (booklet, libretto, itself an Italian diminutive), carretó (wheelbarrow).

examples.en: What a cute little cat!

examples.ca: Viuen en una caseta a la muntanya.
examples.en: They live in a little house in the mountains.
He’s bought himself a massive car.
Hang on, just a minute.

title: Word formation: -ció, -ment, -itat, -dor, -ble
summary: How to make new words from verbs and adjectives you already know.
explanation:
Good news: most of these suffixes have English cousins, so many words are easy to guess. The traps are gender and spelling.

Nouns from verbs:

  • -ció / -sió (fem.), English -tion / -sion: organitzar → organització, decidir → decisió. The accent disappears in the plural: organitzacions, decisions.
  • -ment (masc.), used far more widely than English -ment: desenvolupar → desenvolupament (development), pagar → pagament (payment), néixer → naixement (birth), créixer → creixement (growth)
  • -dor / -dora, English -er, a person or a machine: treballar → treballador (worker), rentar → rentadora (washing machine)

Don’t confuse the noun suffix -ment with the adverb ending -ment, the Catalan equivalent of English -ly, which is added to the feminine adjective: ràpida → ràpidament (quickly).

Nouns from adjectives: -itat / -etat / -tat (fem.), English -ity: possible → possibilitat, lliure → llibertat; also -esa (fem.), often English -ness: bo → bonesa (goodness), trist → tristesa (sadness).

Adjectives from verbs: -ble (“that can be …”), English -able / -ible: menjar → menjable, creure → creïble, llegir → llegible. The prefix in- / im- / il- makes them negative: impossible, increïble, il·legible. Note the diaeresis in creïble and the l·l in il·legible, where English illegible has a plain double l.

Adjectives from nouns: -ós / -osa, English -ous: perill → perillós (dangerous), orgull → orgullós (proud).

examples.en: The decision is final.
It’s incredible!

examples.ca: El creixement de la ciutat és ràpid.
examples.en: The city is growing fast.
This handwriting is illegible.

title: Written accents: à, è, é, ò, ó
summary: When to write an accent, and which one: open or closed.
explanation:
English has no written accents, so it’s tempting to treat Catalan ones as decoration. They aren’t: an accent marks the stressed syllable whenever the general rule wouldn’t predict it, and on e and o it also shows the vowel sound. Leaving one out is a spelling mistake and can even change the word: pública (public) vs publica (publishes).

Where depends on which syllable is stressed:

  • stress on the last syllable: write an accent if the word ends in a vowel, a vowel + s, or -en, -in: cafè, també, francès, català, entén, Berlín (but not -ens, -ins: entens, camins)
  • stress on the second-to-last syllable: write an accent only if the word does not end that way: fàcil, difícil, àrab, telèfon, exàmens
  • stress on the third-to-last syllable: always write it: música, pàgina, Mònica

Which mark:

  • a: always grave, à
  • e, o: grave è, ò for an open vowel (è roughly as in bed, ò like a short version of the vowel in British law), acute é, ó for a closed one (as in say and go, but without the glide): cafè / també, això / cançó
  • i, u: always acute, í, ú

If you know some Spanish, beware: Spanish only uses the acute, but Catalan writes à (català, never “catalá”) and distinguishes è from é.

Since the 2016 spelling reform only 15 diacritic accents remain, which simply tell apart two words that are otherwise spelt the same: és / es, són / son, mà / ma, més / mes, sí / si, etc. Words such as soc (I am), os (bone) and net (grandson) no longer take one.

examples.ca: El francès és fàcil? Més que l’àrab!
examples.en: Is French easy? Easier than Arabic!
She listens to music too.
Yes, if you like.

title: Apostrophe and contractions: l’, d’, al, del
summary: When to shorten the article and the preposition.
explanation:
In English the apostrophe marks contractions and possession (don’t, Anna’s). In Catalan it marks elision: a short word loses its vowel before another vowel. Unlike English contractions, this is compulsory, even in the most formal writing.

el, la, de are shortened before a vowel or h (which is always silent in Catalan): l’home, l’escola, d’Andorra, d’aquí.

la is not shortened before unstressed i, u, hi, hu: la universitat, la història, la humanitat, la idea (but l’illa, l’única, l’ira (anger), where the i/u is stressed). El has no such exception: l’hivern, l’univers.

La is not shortened either before the names of letters (la a, la essa) or in a few fixed cases such as la una (one o’clock).

Contractions: a + el = al, de + el = del, per + el = pel, and in the plural als, dels, pels. They only happen with masculine el / els, never with la: a la, de la. Before a vowel there is no contraction, because the article is elided instead: de l’home, a l’escola.

Another difference from English: Catalan (especially in Catalonia) puts an article before first names, so Anna’s car is el cotxe de l’Anna.

Pronouns are elided too: m’agrada, t’estimo, l’he vist, n’hi ha.

examples.en: I’m going to the hospital.
I study at university.

examples.ca: El cotxe de l’Anna és vermell.
examples.en: Anna’s car is red.
It’s one o’clock.

exercises.instruction: Fill in el, la, l’ or del, de l’, al, a l’.

title: What time is it? Catalan “quarters”
summary: Un quart de nou, dos quarts de deu, and the modern alternative.
explanation:
On the hour: És la una. Són les dues, les tres… The word hora / hores is understood, hence the feminine article.

English counts from the hour that has passed (a quarter past eight). The traditional Catalan system counts quarters of the coming hour:

  • 8:15 = un quart de nou (one quarter of the way to nine)
  • 8:30 = dos quarts de nou (two quarters of the way to nine)
  • 8:45 = tres quarts de nou
  • 8:20 = un quart i cinc de nou; 8:55 = les nou menys cinc (five to nine)
  • around 8:07 = mig quart de nou

The big trap: dos quarts de nou is 8:30, not 9:30. If you’re used to British half nine (= 9:30), be extra careful: Catalan works the other way round, like German halb neun. The verb agrees: És un quart de nou, but Són dos quarts de nou.

Alongside it there is a simpler system counting from the current hour, as in English, which everyone understands: les vuit i quart, les vuit i mitja, les nou menys quart.

Questions: Quina hora és? (What time is it?) A quina hora…? (What time…?) Answers: A les nou. A un quart de deu. Before una and onze, de becomes d’: dos quarts d’una (12:30), tres quarts d’onze (10:45).

examples.ca: Quina hora és? Són dos quarts de cinc.
examples.en: What time is it? It’s half past four.

examples.ca: El tren surt a tres quarts de vuit.
examples.en: The train leaves at 7:45.
See you at one.
It’s five to ten.

exercises.instruction: Write the time using the traditional Catalan system.

title: Ordinal numbers and dates
summary: Primer, segon, tercer… and how to say the date.
explanation:
Ordinals: primer, segon, tercer, quart, then the suffix -è: cinquè, sisè, setè, vuitè, novè, desè. Feminine: primera, segona, tercera, quarta, cinquena… Abbreviated, like English 1st, 2nd: 1r, 2n, 3r, 4t, 5è; feminine 1a, 2a, 3a…

Dates: English uses ordinals (the 23rd of April, April 23rd), but Catalan uses ordinary cardinal numbers: el + number + de + month, with elision before a vowel:

  • el 23 d’abril (el vint-i-tres d’abril), l’11 de setembre, el 5 de juny
  • the 1st: l’u de maig or el primer de maig, the only day that can take an ordinal

Months and days of the week are written with a small letter: dilluns, 5 de juny, not “Dilluns” or “Juny”.

Asking and answering: Quin dia és avui? Avui som a 5 de juny (or És el 5 de juny).

Years are read as one whole number, not in pairs as in English (nineteen ninety): el 1990 = “el mil nou-cents noranta”, el 2026 = “el dos mil vint-i-sis”. Use the article where English says “in”: Va néixer el 1990. Decades: als anys noranta (in the nineties).

Floors are counted from above the ground floor (planta baixa), as in British English, so el tercer pis is what Americans would call the fourth floor.

examples.en: I live on the third floor.
St George’s Day is on the 23rd of April.
He was born in 1990.

examples.ca: És la primera vegada que vinc.
examples.en: It’s the first time I’ve been here.

items.a: l’u de maig / el primer de maig
